stem.text: The diagram shows a possible outcome for an economy.

stem.alt: An environmental Kuznets curve diagram: an inverted-U-shaped curve with level of environmental degradation on the vertical axis and per capita income on the horizontal axis, starting low near the origin, rising to a peak marked X, then falling toward a point Y slightly past the peak, and continuing to fall as per capita income keeps rising.

stem.text: What is the most likely reason why an economy is unable to turn at point X towards point Y?

options.text: a cut in direct taxes causes a substitution effect and tax revenues continue to rise
a depreciation of the exchange rate increases the rate of economic growth
pollution continues to be caused by rising real GDP
there is now greater emphasis on living standards rather than economic growth

explanation.text: The environmental Kuznets curve predicts environmental degradation rises with income at low income levels, then falls once income passes a turning point (as a country can afford cleaner technology, stronger regulation and a shift toward less polluting services). An economy fails to turn from X toward Y when economic growth keeps happening in ways that keep generating pollution at the same or a growing rate — i.e. rising real GDP continues to directly cause pollution, rather than growth increasingly coming from cleaner sources or being matched by stronger environmental protection.

optionAnalysis.text: A cut in direct taxes and rising tax revenue describes a fiscal/labour-supply effect, unrelated to whether growth is accompanied by pollution or by cleaner technology and regulation.
A depreciation increasing growth describes a trade/exchange-rate channel of growth, not a reason growth continues to generate pollution rather than reduce it.

If pollution keeps being generated directly by the growth process itself (rising real GDP), the economy stays on the upward/flat part of the curve rather than turning down toward lower degradation at point Y.

Greater emphasis on living standards over pure growth would, if anything, help an economy turn toward reduced environmental degradation (toward Y), not prevent it — this describes a reason the turn would happen, not a reason it fails to.

reasoningChain: Recall the environmental Kuznets curve hypothesis: degradation rises then falls as income grows, once sufficiently high income allows cleaner growth.
Identify that turning from X to Y requires growth to decouple from pollution (e.g. through regulation, cleaner technology, structural shift to services).
Recognise that if rising real GDP continues to directly cause pollution (no such decoupling occurs), the economy cannot turn downward and stays stuck near or past the peak.
Rule out the other options as describing unrelated fiscal, exchange-rate or preference-based mechanisms that do not explain a failure of the pollution-income relationship to reverse.

inferredMistakes.text: Picking an option (D) that actually describes a reason the economy *would* successfully turn toward Y (valuing living standards, which usually includes environmental quality), rather than a reason it fails to turn.
